title: Ponticianus' story (Confessions 8.6)
hookLine: a visitor tells of Antony, and Augustine is ashamed he's still stuck
tomorrow: what did a child chant over the garden wall?

lines: A BOOK ON THE GAME TABLE.
cards: A friend finally quits the job she's complained about for years, the same week you're still talking about yours. Augustine got a story like that.
A visitor drops by his house in Milan: Ponticianus, a fellow African with a high post at the emperor's court. He spots a book on the game table, picks it up, and smiles. It's the apostle Paul.
And he starts telling a story, with no idea what it's about to do to his host.

teach.b: First he talks about Antony, the monk of Egypt, amazed they've never heard of him. Then the story he came with. At Trier, he and three companions went walking by the city wall.

Two of them wandered into a small house where some servants of God lived, and found a book: the life of Antony. One began to read, and something caught fire. A friend of God, he said, if I want it, look, I become one now.
Both stayed. As Ponticianus spoke, Augustine says, God turned him around to face himself. He saw his stalling, and he was ashamed.
Years before, he admits, he had prayed: give me chastity and self-control, but not yet. So here's a question churches answer differently.
Some tell faith as a moment, a day you can name. Their best case: not yet can be a quiet no, and two officers changed in an afternoon.
Others tell it as growth over a lifetime, in prayer, worship and community.
Their best case: Augustine had circled for years before this, and those years counted too. Some churches ask for a testimony of the moment you decided; others speak more of a long road.
Augustine's story holds both: years of stalling, and a now that's coming.

how: Christians have passed on the lives of saints like Antony to encourage one another, and churches differ on whether they ask people to name a moment of decision or speak of faith growing over a lifetime.

o: a sermon Augustine preached in Milan
a visitor's tale that showed Augustine his stalling
a letter Augustine sent to a friend in Rome

p: a visitor from the emperor's court
give me self-control, but not yet

s: Augustine already knew Antony's story before this visit
Ponticianus is amazed they've never heard of him.
Augustine once prayed for self-control, but not yet
he admits it: give me chastity and continence, only not yet.
for Christians, faith only counts if you can name the day
the popular belief. some tell it as a moment, some as a lifetime; churches differ.

games.q: a church friend says real faith has a moment you can name. yours grew slowly. state her view at its strongest.
o: slow faith doesn't count, so yours isn't real faith.
'not yet' can quietly mean no; a now gets you off the fence.
moments are just more exciting to tell in church.
games.why: that's the best case for the moment: Augustine's own 'not yet' was stalling. the slow view has one too: his years of circling counted.

practice: Get up and walk slowly for a minute, the way the friends at Trier walked by the wall, and let one story of someone who changed come to mind. Ask it one question: what am I still saying not yet to?
Then sit, and let the answer stay as it comes.

wordCard.voice: Ponticianus' story. A visitor's tale of two court officers who changed in an afternoon, and Augustine, still saying not yet.

orig.note: Latin: look, now I become one. the court officer's words in Confessions 8.6: a friend of God, if I want it, ecce nunc fio.

carryVoice: Your line: why not now? Augustine is about to ask it out loud. Catch you tomorrow.
